strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper empirically demonstrates that text conditions, which succeed in other vision tasks, are ineffective or even harmful for robotic control, and supports this with cross-attention map analysis (Fig. 3) showing grounding failures on tasks like Cheetah-run.

The proposed ORCA framework (learnable task prompts + frame-specific visual prompts from dense DINOv2 features) is simple, conceptually sound, and validated end-to-end with a standard behavior cloning objective.

Strong empirical coverage: 12 tasks across three benchmarks (DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, Adroit), three seeds with standard deviations reported, and consistent SOTA improvements over task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive (Text, CoOp, TADP) baselines.

Thorough ablations that isolate the contribution of each component (Table 4), the layer-selection choice (Table 5), and the diffusion timestep (Table 6), which strengthens the empirical case and aids reproducibility.

Attention visualization (Fig. 6) provides interpretable evidence that task prompts capture global task-relevant regions while visual prompts capture dynamic, frame-specific details, connecting the method to its motivation.
Good reproducibility documentation, including pseudocode for the compression layer (Alg. 1), full text conditions (Table 8), and an efficiency comparison (Table 7).
weaknesses: Margins over the strongest task-adaptive baselines are modest in several settings (e.g., MetaWorld mean 95.2 vs. 93.1 for TADP; DMC mean 74.3 vs. 70.7), and on some tasks all methods tie (MetaWorld Button-press 100.0) or the improvement is within noise given the large standard deviations (e.g., Cheetah-run 50.0 ± 8.4).

The task prompts are essentially per-task learnable token embeddings shared across observations, which is close in spirit to existing prompt-learning approaches such as CoOp; the paper could more explicitly disentangle how much of the gain is attributable to the novel visual prompts versus the task prompts.

The visual prompts rely on an external pretrained encoder (DINOv2), which partially undercuts the framing of extracting task-adaptive representations 'without fine-tuning the model itself'; the contribution of this added frozen encoder versus the diffusion features is not fully isolated.

Inference latency is substantially higher than the closest baselines (48ms vs. 11ms for VC-1 and 26ms for SCR), which matters for real-time control; while reported, this cost is not discussed in terms of practical applicability.

The claim that text conditions are 'ineffective' is supported by only a single VLM (Gemini 2.5) and a single captioning strategy; alternative prompting schemes or more control-specific text formulations are not explored, so the negative conclusion may be narrower than stated.
Evaluation is confined to simulated benchmarks with no real-robot validation, and no comparison against fine-tuning the diffusion model is provided despite the paper's argument against fine-tuning.
Some overclaiming in phrasing (e.g., 'state-of-the-art ... significantly surpassing prior methods') is stronger than what the modest and sometimes high-variance numbers support.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing with a genuinely useful negative result: the paper shows that VLM-generated text conditions, which succeed in visual perception tasks, provide minimal or even negative gains in control (Fig. 1, Fig. 3a), and backs this up with cross-attention visualizations showing noisy grounding on dynamic tasks such as Cheetah-run versus well-grounded attention on Button-press (Fig. 3b/c). This diagnostic analysis is the most novel part of the paper.

The proposed method (ORCA) is simple, principled, and directly follows from the analysis: learnable task prompts shared across observations to avoid erroneous grounding, plus dense visual prompts from DINOv2 projected through a small conv layer to capture frame-specific detail, all trained end-to-end with a behavior-cloning objective without fine-tuning the diffusion model.

Empirical evidence is broad and consistent: 12 tasks across three standard benchmarks (DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, Adroit), with means improving over the strongest task-adaptive baselines (TADP: 70.7 -> 74.3 on DMC; 93.1 -> 95.2 on MetaWorld; 57.3 -> 65.3 on Adroit) and over task-agnostic baselines (VC-1, CLIP, SCR). The gains hold across locomotion, manipulation, and dexterous-hand suites rather than being confined to one setting.

Ablations are thorough and informative: component analysis isolating task vs. visual prompts (Table 4), layer-wise selection of U-Net features (Table 5), diffusion timestep ablation (Table 6), efficiency comparison (Table 7), and an interesting analysis of the null condition showing <bos> attends to background while <eos> tracks salient objects (Fig. 7).

Reproducibility is good for a CVPR submission: the backbone (Stable Diffusion v1.5), feature source (DINOv2), token lengths, compression-layer design (with pseudocode), training schedule, and the full text conditions used by all baselines are provided in the appendix, along with qualitative rollouts for all three suites.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the method assembles existing ingredients (learnable prompt tokens as in CoOp/Textual Inversion, dense features from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, and diffusion-based representations as in SCR). The contribution is primarily empirical and analytical rather than methodological.

A potential confound is not ruled out: the visual prompts are derived from DINOv2, a strong pretrained visual encoder in its own right. There is no ablation that feeds DINOv2 features directly into the policy (bypassing the diffusion model), so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the diffusion conditioning versus simply adding a good visual feature stream.

The broad claim that 'text conditions are ineffective in robotic control' rests on a single captioning strategy with one VLM (Gemini 2.5). The paper itself notes the null condition is already roughly grounded to salient objects, which makes it hard for text to help; a more carefully qualified claim (or additional captioning variants) would strengthen the conclusion.

Statistical support is thin in places: results are averaged over only three seeds, and several per-task deltas fall within overlapping standard deviations (e.g., MetaWorld Bin-picking ties TADP at 90.7 +/- 4.6; Adroit Relocate ties CLIP at 44.0 +/- 4.0). The mean-level improvements are the reliable signal, but per-task wins should not be over-interpreted.
Cost is not negligible: 480M parameters and 48 ms latency versus 11 ms for VC-1 (Table 7), which matters for real-time control; the paper does not discuss this trade-off in depth.

All evaluation is in simulation (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit). Given the paper's framing around 'robotic control,' the absence of any real-robot or hardware-in-the-loop validation limits how strongly the practical claims can be made.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical finding: naive text conditions (from a strong VLM like Gemini 2.5) yield minimal or even negative gains in robotic control, and it supports this with cross-attention visualizations (Fig. 3) that show noisy grounding for tasks like Cheetah-run. This negative result and its analysis are genuinely useful for the community.

The proposed ORCA method is simple, clearly described, and consistently improves over both task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive (Text, CoOp, TADP) baselines across 12 tasks in three benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit). The framework figure (Fig. 4) and the policy-learning objective are easy to follow.

The experimental work is reasonably thorough: three widely-used benchmarks, five seeds' worth of tasks, component ablation (Table 4), layer-selection ablation (Table 5), and timestep ablation (Table 6). The paper also provides cross-attention visualizations for task/visual prompts (Fig. 6) and qualitative rollouts (Figs. 8-10).

Reproducibility is relatively good: the compression-layer pseudocode (Alg. 1), full text prompts (Table 8), baseline details, and implementation hyperparameters (timesteps, token lengths, backbones) are provided.
The paper is well-written and well-organized, with informative figures that communicate the motivation and method effectively.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The two core ingredients — learnable task prompts and visual prompts — correspond closely to existing ideas (learnable prompt/prefix tuning, e.g., CoOp/Textual Inversion, and visual prompting/feature injection). The contribution is largely the combination and its application to control, which limits the conceptual advance relative to prior work the paper itself cites.

A critical ablation is missing: the visual prompt is built from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, but there is no baseline that simply feeds DINOv2 (or DINOv2 + SD) features directly to the policy without the diffusion-conditioning machinery. As written, it is unclear how much of the gain is attributable to the diffusion model versus the injected DINOv2 features, which weakens the paper's central framing of 'diffusion models for control.'

The improvements over the strongest task-adaptive baselines are modest in several settings and sometimes within noise. On DMC, ORCA (74.3) vs. TADP (70.7); on MetaWorld, 95.2 vs. 93.1; on Adroit Relocate, ORCA (44.0) is identical to CLIP (44.0) and the Adroit mean gain is driven almost entirely by Pen. In Table 4, task-prompt-only actually degrades Cheetah-run (38.9 vs. 43.4 for the null baseline), suggesting the individual components are not independently beneficial and the benefit is largely interaction-driven.

Only three seeds are used, and standard deviations are large (e.g., Cheetah-run 50.0 ± 8.4; Text 38.8 ± 5.9; Adroit CLIP 44.0 ± 4.0). Claims such as 'significantly surpassing prior methods' and 'new state-of-the-art' are therefore not strongly supported statistically, and several reported differences fall within one standard deviation.
Evaluation is confined to simulated benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) with no real-robot validation, limiting the demonstrated impact for a robotics-control contribution.

The efficiency analysis (Table 7) shows ORCA is substantially slower (48 ms vs. 11 ms for VC-1, ~4x), and the paper does not meaningfully discuss this trade-off or whether the gains justify the added compute/latency.

strengths: Provides a clear and well-motivated study of conditioning diffusion models for robotic control, identifying that naive text conditions are often ineffective and analyzing this via cross-attention maps (Fig. 3).

Proposes a simple, parameter-efficient approach (ORCA) that learns task and visual prompts while keeping the diffusion model frozen, requiring only 10.6M learnable parameters versus roughly 302M for full fine-tuning (Table 3).
Reports consistent and substantial gains across 12 tasks on DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, outperforming CLIP, VC-1, SCR, text baselines, CoOp, and TADP (Tables 1, 2).
Includes extensive ablations on component design, layer selection, diffusion timestep, and vision encoder choice, as well as an additional LIBERO-Long evaluation (Tables 4, 5, A-D, E; Fig. A).
The cross-attention visualizations in Fig. 6 provide useful qualitative evidence that task prompts capture task-relevant regions while visual prompts capture frame-specific dynamics.
The paper is generally well written, with detailed appendix material covering text descriptions, baseline details, compression layer pseudocode, and additional quantitative results.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method essentially combines existing ideas from prompt tuning, visual prompting, and diffusion feature extraction for control, and its main contribution is an empirical recipe rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The claim that text conditions are ineffective in robotic control is supported mainly by one VLM-generated caption set and simple task-name prompts on SD v1.5; stronger prompt engineering, different text encoders, or retrieval-based text conditions are not explored.

Important baselines are missing, including diffusion-policy methods such as Diffusion Policy/DP3 and recent VLA models such as OpenVLA or Octo, which limits the strength of the state-of-the-art claim.

The visual prompts depend on an external frozen vision encoder (DINOv2), and the visual tokens are fed through a frozen text encoder, which is somewhat unnatural and complicates the claim that conditioning the diffusion model is the primary source of improvement.
All experiments are conducted in simulated benchmarks; no real-robot evaluation is provided, despite the paper's focus on robotic control.
Efficiency is worse than some baselines in latency (48 ms vs. 11 ms for VC-1 and 26 ms for SCR) and total model size (480.1M parameters), which may matter for real-time control.
Some reproducibility details are limited: no code release is mentioned, and key training hyperparameters and policy architecture details are not fully specified in the main paper.

strengths: Provides a systematic study of conditioning mechanisms for frozen text-to-image diffusion models in robotic control, with a clear and well-motivated problem statement.

Identifies an important empirical phenomenon: text conditions generated by a state-of-the-art VLM are often ineffective or even harmful in control tasks, supported by cross-attention visualizations that reveal poor grounding in dynamic control environments.

Proposes ORCA, a simple yet effective framework that learns task prompts and visual prompts to condition a frozen diffusion model in a task-adaptive and frame-sensitive manner, avoiding expensive diffusion fine-tuning.
Achieves strong empirical results across 12 tasks on DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, Adroit, and LIBERO-Long, outperforming relevant baselines such as CLIP, VC-1, SCR, CoOp, and TADP.
Demonstrates favorable parameter efficiency: ORCA uses only 10.6M learnable parameters while outperforming full fine-tuning approaches that require hundreds of millions of learnable parameters.
Includes thorough ablations on prompt components, layer selection, diffusion timesteps, vision encoder choice, and efficiency, along with extensive qualitative visualizations and appendix details.
The paper is clearly written, with helpful figures, detailed implementation notes, and reproducible experimental settings using standard benchmarks and multiple seeds.
weaknesses: The claim that text conditions are broadly 'ineffective' in robotic control may be somewhat overstated: it is based on captions from a single VLM (Gemini 2.5) and does not explore human-crafted frame-wise descriptions or more extensive prompt engineering, so the conclusion about text conditioning in general may be too strong.

The method relies on an additional pre-trained vision encoder (DINOv2) for visual prompts, and the ablation shows a substantial drop without it (54.7 vs. 65.3 on Adroit), making it unclear how much of the gain comes from diffusion conditioning versus external visual features. A cleaner isolation of the diffusion model's contribution would strengthen the claims.

Important visual-representation and control baselines such as R3M, MVP, and recent diffusion-policy methods (e.g., DP/DP3) are not compared in the main experiments, even though they are highly relevant to the paper's claims about state-of-the-art robotic control performance.

The learned task prompts are not directly compared against simpler alternatives such as a task-ID embedding or FiLM-style task conditioning, so it is unclear whether the text-encoder-based prompt learning is necessary for the observed gains.
Evaluation is entirely in simulated benchmarks; no real-robot experiments are provided, which limits the evidence for real-world applicability despite strong simulation results.

Some design choices (e.g., diffusion timestep t=0, concatenation of down/mid blocks, prompt lengths) are selected empirically without deep analysis, and the method may require per-task hyperparameter tuning.
The paper does not release code or model checkpoints in the provided manuscript, which may hinder reproducibility in practice even though implementation details are relatively detailed.

strengths: The paper identifies and investigates an interesting and underexplored question: how to effectively condition text-to-image diffusion models for robotic control, and it offers a plausible analysis (with cross-attention visualizations in Fig. 3) of why machine-generated text captions can be ineffective or even harmful in control domains.

The empirical evaluation is broad and reasonably rigorous: 12 tasks across DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, and Adroit, plus LIBERO-Long in the supplement, with three seeds and standard deviations, and comparisons against task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive (Text, CoOp, TADP) baselines.

The ablation suite is thorough, covering component contributions (task vs visual prompts), U-Net layer selection, diffusion timestep, choice of external vision encoder, and alternative diffusion backbones (SVD, SD 3.0), as well as a parameter-efficiency comparison against full fine-tuning and LoRA.

The writing is clear, the method is simply described, and the appendix provides implementation details (compression layer pseudocode, full text conditions, baseline specifications) that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The proposed ORCA essentially combines existing ideas—learnable prompt tokens (CoOp/Textual Inversion) and dense visual tokens from a frozen encoder—and applies them to a frozen Stable Diffusion model for control. This is an incremental combination rather than a new mechanism.

The central motivating claim—that text conditions are ineffective for robotic control—is supported by only a single VLM (Gemini 2.5) and a single captioning pipeline, and the failures are attributed to a vague 'domain gap.' It is not established that this reflects a fundamental limitation of text conditioning rather than a weakness of the specific caption generator or prompt design, which weakens the paper's core narrative.

The 'task-adaptive diffusion representation' framing is partly undermined by the method's own ablation. Table C shows that removing the external DINOv2 encoder drops Adroit performance from 65.3 to 54.7, indicating the key benefit comes largely from a frozen pre-trained visual encoder—the same class of 'task-agnostic frozen representation' the paper critiques—rather than from the diffusion model itself.

Performance gains over the strongest task-adaptive baselines are modest in several benchmarks (e.g., MetaWorld mean 95.2 vs. 93.1 for TADP; DMC mean 74.3 vs. 70.6 for CoOp), and no statistical significance testing is reported, so it is unclear whether the improvements are robust or within noise given the large standard deviations on some tasks.

The method requires learning prompts during downstream policy training, and the visual-prompt benefit appears to depend on an added DINOv2 encoder and projection layers, making the pipeline heavier and less clearly attributable to the proposed conditioning scheme; latency (48 ms) is also notably higher than VC-1 (11 ms) and SCR (26 ms).

Some supporting analysis is qualitative and speculative, e.g., the interpretation of attention maps in Fig. 6 and the attribution of <bos>/<eos> behavior in Fig. A, which are not quantitatively validated and could be over-interpreted.
